# Assessments {.unnumbered}

## Assignment I

- **Title:** Programmed Map and Cartographic Critique
- **Type:** Coursework
- Due date: 5th November 2026 (week 6)
- 40% of the final mark
- Chance to be reassessed
- Electronic submission only

This assignment has two parts. **Part A (10% of final grade)** is a short, individual, non-coding critique of the classification scheme of one published map: three maps will be on Canvas and you choose one, writing no more than 300 words. **Part B (30% of final grade)** is the programmed map: you will map population density by region in China, then the population change between 2015 and 2025, and write up to 500 words about the choices you made.

Both parts, plus a **mandatory AI-use declaration**, are submitted together in one `.html` file. If the declaration is missing from your rendered html you can lose up to 10 marks.

- Full Assignment details [here](https://theuniversityofliverpool-my.sharepoint.com/:b:/g/personal/pietrost_liverpool_ac_uk/IQCW74t4Ndg8Qp-NWy-aOIfFAbR5Lp4YUeZQfhf_OQVEvZk?e=OVDksJ)

You will submit an `.html` file obtained by rendering your `.qmd` in `R` or `.ipynb` Jupyter Notebook in `Python`.

- If you are doing the assignment in `R`: You can start from this [**.qmd file**](https://theuniversityofliverpool-my.sharepoint.com/:u:/g/personal/pietrost_liverpool_ac_uk/IQCEP3xC0cPeTqFhk394LBgnAXazecIuU8o2Ra2uTy7xdFU?e=5NqmTC) to render the `html`. Other file formats will not be accepted.

- If you are doing the assignment in `Python`: start from this [**.ipynb**](https://theuniversityofliverpool-my.sharepoint.com/:u:/g/personal/pietrost_liverpool_ac_uk/IQApTU-FTDEAT4rk0-hmJzcyAeyyNFZTm-WGTlxXcOtWDXE?e=XThvaV). Before exporting, restart the kernel and run all cells (`Kernel –> Restart Kernel and Run All Cells`), then `File –> Save and Export Notebook As... –> HTML`. Other file formats will not be accepted.

### Submit

One html file: a rendered `.qmd` with R code, or a rendered Jupyter notebook with Python code, containing your AI-use declaration, Part A and Part B.

### Evaluation

**Part A** is marked on how accurately you identify the classification scheme, how well you link its strengths and weaknesses to the data and the map's message, and how convincingly you justify an alternative.

**Part B** is marked on three pillars:

1.  **Data processing and code quality:** your proficiency in handling and manipulating data, and writing code a reader can follow — a logical sequence of steps, sensible names, comments explaining why, no dead or duplicated code, and no clutter in the rendered document.

2.  **Map assemblage:** your ability to master technologies that allow you to create a compelling map.

3.  **Design and narrative:** your success in designing an appealing map with a compelling narrative.

## Assignment II

- **Title:** Computational Essay
- **Type:** Coursework
- Due date: 10th December 2026 (week 11)
- 60% of the final mark
- Chance to be reassessed
- Electronic submission only

A computational essay on Airbnb and neighbourhoods in the **San Francisco Bay Area**. You take the role of a geographic data scientist exploring "old" (US census) and "new" (Inside Airbnb) forms of spatial data, combining code, data visualisation and prose, supported by references. Maximum **1,000 words** of ordinary text, up to **five** maps or figures and **one** table; references, code and the AI-use declaration do not count towards the word limit.

- **Part 1** (everyone): Airbnb prices by ZCTA, set against an **AI-generated map made with no input data** (Map 1); Airbnb prices combined with one socio-economic variable from the American Community Survey (Map 2); and spatial autocorrelation (Map 3).
- **Part 2** (choose one): a geodemographic classification, a regionalisation, or OpenStreetMap points of interest clustered with DBSCAN.

Your essay must open with the completed **AI-use declaration** from the template, even if you used no AI tools. If it is missing from your rendered html you can lose up to 10 marks.

- Full Assignment details [here](https://theuniversityofliverpool-my.sharepoint.com/:b:/r/personal/pietrost_liverpool_ac_uk/_layouts/15/onedrive.aspx?id=%2Fpersonal%2Fpietrost%5Fliverpool%5Fac%5Fuk%2FDocuments%2FENVS363%5F563%5F2026%2FAssignments%2FENVS363%5F563%2E2%5F26%5F27%2Epdf&parent=%2Fpersonal%2Fpietrost%5Fliverpool%5Fac%5Fuk%2FDocuments%2FENVS363%5F563%5F2026%2FAssignments&share=cQo2K0doMho7SbM76Hgkac6DEgUCWJXHVcxy7guCwHZexK4Bxg)

You will submit an `.html` file obtained by rendering your `.qmd` in `R` or `.ipynb` Jupyter Notebook in `Python`. Use the same language as Assignment I.

- If you are doing the assignment in `R`: start from this [**ENVS2627-363-563.2.qmd file**](https://theuniversityofliverpool-my.sharepoint.com/:u:/r/personal/pietrost_liverpool_ac_uk/_layouts/15/onedrive.aspx?id=%2Fpersonal%2Fpietrost%5Fliverpool%5Fac%5Fuk%2FDocuments%2FENVS363%5F563%5F2026%2FAssignments%2FENVS2627%2D363%2D563%2E2%2Eqmd&parent=%2Fpersonal%2Fpietrost%5Fliverpool%5Fac%5Fuk%2FDocuments%2FENVS363%5F563%5F2026%2FAssignments&share=cQr1cSWqtt%5FhT7qCbhyqIdXWEgUCWe8P0NDqkEkhQMKXMYMp8w) to render the `html`. Other file formats will not be accepted.

- If you are doing the assignment in `Python`: start from this [**ENVS2627-363-563.2.ipynb**](https://theuniversityofliverpool-my.sharepoint.com/:u:/r/personal/pietrost_liverpool_ac_uk/_layouts/15/onedrive.aspx?id=%2Fpersonal%2Fpietrost%5Fliverpool%5Fac%5Fuk%2FDocuments%2FENVS363%5F563%5F2026%2FAssignments%2FENVS2627%2D363%2D563%2E2%2Eipynb&parent=%2Fpersonal%2Fpietrost%5Fliverpool%5Fac%5Fuk%2FDocuments%2FENVS363%5F563%5F2026%2FAssignments&share=cQrxR4yCULNrSr8uR3CPyU2lEgUCOKaVAgUuPZ5x%2DKG2ryiaYA). Before exporting, restart the kernel and run all cells (`Kernel –> Restart Kernel and Run All Cells`), then `File –> Save and Export Notebook As... –> HTML`. Other file formats will not be accepted.

### Data

- **Inside Airbnb:** download `listings.csv.gz` and `neighbourhoods.geojson` for San Francisco, San Mateo County and Oakland from [Inside Airbnb](https://insideairbnb.com/get-the-data/), and report the snapshot dates you used. The templates do this for you. Read the [data assumptions](https://insideairbnb.com/data-assumptions/) before interpreting the data.
- **American Community Survey 2020–2024 (5-year), census tracts:** retrieve it through the US Census API, using [`tidycensus`](https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/articles/basic-usage.html) in R or [`pygris`](https://walker-data.com/pygris/) in Python. All variables are listed [here](https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/variables.html).
- **ZCTAs** (2020 boundaries): download with `tigris::zctas()` in R or `pygris.zctas()` in Python.

::: callout-important
## Census API key

Request a free key [here](https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html) and click the activation link in the email you receive: the key does not work until it is activated. Store it once, in the Console, **never in your `.qmd` or notebook** (it would appear in the html you submit):

- R: `tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR_KEY", install = TRUE)`, then restart R.
- Python: save it as an environment variable called `CENSUS_API_KEY`.

If you see an error mentioning `<html` or `invalid char in json text`, the API has rejected your key: check it is activated and that you restarted R.
:::

**Not using the API?** A ready-made set of ACS variables for the study area is available in the [ACS_bayarea data folder](https://github.com/GDSL-UL/gds/tree/main/data/ACS_bayarea). Read `GEOID` as text, or you will lose its leading zero.

- [ACS_bayarea_2020_2024_tracts.gpkg](https://github.com/GDSL-UL/gds/raw/main/data/ACS_bayarea/ACS_bayarea_2020_2024_tracts.gpkg): tract boundaries with all variables (use this one if you can)
- [ACS_bayarea_2020_2024_vars.csv](https://github.com/GDSL-UL/gds/raw/main/data/ACS_bayarea/ACS_bayarea_2020_2024_vars.csv): the same table without geometry
- [ACS_bayarea_2020_2024_codebook.csv](https://github.com/GDSL-UL/gds/raw/main/data/ACS_bayarea/ACS_bayarea_2020_2024_codebook.csv): what each column means

The column `in_study_area` flags the tracts covered by the Airbnb files (San Francisco, San Mateo County and the City of Oakland).

**ENVS563** students must also source at least two additional datasets on San Francisco or the Bay Area, for example from [DataSF](https://datasf.org/opendata/), [Oakland open data](https://data.oaklandca.gov/), [San Mateo County open data](https://data.smcgov.org/) or [MTC/ABAG](https://opendata.mtc.ca.gov/).

### Resources

- [What is a computational essay?](https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2017/11/what-is-a-computational-essay/) (Stephen Wolfram)
- [Quarto guide](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/)
- [biscale: bivariate mapping in R](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/biscale/vignettes/biscale.html)

**There are three kinds of elements in a computational essay:**

1.  Ordinary text (in English)

2.  Computer input (R or Python)

3.  Computer output

These three elements all work together to express what's being communicated.

## Marking Criteria

This course follows the standard marking criteria (the general ones and those relating to GIS assignments in particular) set by the School of Environmental Sciences. Please make sure to check the student handbook and familiarise with them. In addition to these generic criteria, the following specific criteria will be used in cases where computer code is part of the work being assessed:

- 0-15: the code does not run and there is no documentation to follow it.
- 16-39: the code does not run, or runs but it does not produce the expected outcome. There is some documentation explaining its logic.
- 40-49: the code runs and produces the expected output. There is some documentation explaining its logic.
- 50-59: the code runs and produces the expected output. There is extensive documentation explaining its logic.
- 60-69: the code runs and produces the expected output. There is extensive documentation, properly formatted, explaining its logic.
- 70-79: all as above, plus the code design includes clear evidence of skills presented in advanced sections of the course (e.g. custom methods, list comprehensions, etc.).
- 80-100: all as above, plus the code contains novel contributions that extend/improve the functionality the student was provided with (e.g. algorithm optimizations, novel methods to perform the task, etc.).

## Generative Artificial Intelligence

::: callout-warning
## Prohibited use

You are reminded that **inappropriate use of Generative AI tools** (e.g. ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot) in the preparation of this assignment is **prohibited**. Submitting code, analysis, or narrative that **you cannot explain or justify yourself** will be treated as an **Academic Integrity concern** — regardless of whether AI was involved.
:::

::: callout-important
## Declaration required

You **must submit a short declaration** with your assignment stating:

- **Which** AI tools you used
- **For which parts** of the work (narrative text and/or code)
- **How** you used them (e.g. debugging support, syntax lookup, translation, proof-reading) — versus what you produced yourself

**Undisclosed use discovered later will be treated as an Academic Integrity penalty**, not merely a missing declaration.
:::

::: callout-note
## Narrative sections

Narrative sections should be prepared **substantially in your own words**.

- Ordinary spelling/grammar checks in word-processing packages **do not** need declaring.
- AI proof-reading that **materially changes wording or sentence structure does** need declaring — and **extensive use of it may still incur a penalty even when declared**.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Code

AI coding assistants **may be used for support**, but every part of your submitted code must be **something you can explain and justify in your own words**.
:::

```{=html}
<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
  var noneBox = document.getElementById("none-used");
  if (!noneBox) return;
  var otherBoxes = document.querySelectorAll(".ai-checklist input[type='checkbox']:not(#none-used)");
  var otherTexts = document.querySelectorAll(".ai-inline-text");
  noneBox.addEventListener("change", function () {
    if (noneBox.checked) {
      otherBoxes.forEach(function (b) { b.checked = false; b.disabled = true; });
      otherTexts.forEach(function (t) { t.value = ""; t.disabled = true; });
    } else {
      otherBoxes.forEach(function (b) { b.disabled = false; });
      otherTexts.forEach(function (t) { t.disabled = false; });
    }
  });
});
</script>
```
